A learner asked Big Doug if he ever gets nervous. He said 'never,' then reached for the handle. They were still in the driveway. In park.
Big Doug once rode through an entire chinook. Left Calgary in a parka, got to Airdrie in a T-shirt. Same drive. Same learner. Same confused moose.
Big Doug keeps a mental map of every pothole in Edmonton. It's not a map anymore. It's a six-volume encyclopedia.
Big Doug can tell how a drive will go in ten seconds. If the learner sets the mirrors before touching the radio, it's going to be a beauty.
Big Doug never criticizes a parking job. He just says 'interesting choice' and lets the silence do the rest.
Big Doug once sat through a three-point turn that took eleven points. Full marks for effort. Partial marks for geometry.
Big Doug keeps a granola bar in the glovebox for every learner. Not for snacks. For after the first highway merge. It's a ceremony.
Learner: 'Did I do okay?' Big Doug: 'You did great.' Learner: 'Then why are you holding the handle?' Big Doug: 'Habit, bud. Twenty years of habit.'
Big Doug has been through so many roundabouts in the passenger seat that he gets dizzy watching a ceiling fan.
Before every drive, Big Doug leans way over so the learner can see past his antlers in the mirror. He calls it 'moving the furniture.'
Big Doug rates every parallel park from one to four hooves. In twenty years, nobody has gotten four. A few have gotten 'let's try that again.'
Big Doug has helped so many teens back out of the same driveway that the neighbours wave at him by name.
Big Doug has survived twenty winters in passenger seats. His one true fear: a mall parking lot on the Saturday before Christmas.
Big Doug's review of every learner's first drive: 'Slow, careful and absolutely beautiful. You can let go of the wheel now, bud. We're parked.'
Big Doug says the passenger seat is the best seat in the car. Great view, no responsibility and nobody expects you to know where the gas cap is.
Big Doug calls the first highway drive 'the quiet ride.' Nobody talks. Nobody breathes. Then somebody says 'we did it' and the whole car cheers.
Big Doug's review after a perfect parallel park: 'Beauty. Now do it again so I know it wasn't luck.'
Big Doug has been riding shotgun since flip phones. He's watched cars learn to beep, talk and park themselves. Learners still need practice. So do the cars.
Big Doug doesn't give seatbelt reminders. He just clicks his own belt very loudly and stares straight ahead until you do.
Big Doug has a sixth sense for a skipped shoulder check. His left ear twitches. Twenty years. Never wrong.
The hardest part of Big Doug's job is pretending he didn't notice you put the car in reverse when you meant drive. He noticed. He's a professional.
One learner backed out of the driveway so slowly that a gopher dug a new tunnel, moved in and started a family. Big Doug was there. He brought snacks.
A learner asked Big Doug for his best winter tip. He handed over a toque, a scraper and a granola bar. 'The rest,' he said, 'is patience.'
Learner: 'Do I signal here?' Big Doug: 'What do you think?' Learner: signals. Big Doug: 'Beauty. You knew all along.'
Big Doug's secret to supervising is a calm face. On the inside: a full moose stampede. On the outside: 'nice and easy, bud.'
Every learner's first lap of a parking lot sounds the same from the passenger seat: soft brake, tiny gasp, nervous laugh, 'okay, again.' Big Doug loves it.
Big Doug calls a perfect three-point turn a hat trick. He tosses his trucker cap onto the back seat and everything.
Big Doug's least favourite place is an underground parkade. Every time a learner drives under a clearance bar, he ducks. He's inside the car. He ducks anyway.
Big Doug never calls shotgun. He doesn't need to. Twenty years in that seat. He has seniority.
Big Doug's favourite road trip game is 'spot the moose.' He wins every time. He just checks the side mirror.
Big Doug has supervised learners through hail, chinooks, ice fog and one snowstorm in June. The learners got better. The weather never did.
Twenty years riding shotgun and Big Doug has one request for parents: if you're going to gasp, gasp at something real. One mom gasped at a leaf.
Twenty years riding shotgun taught Big Doug patience. Twenty years of little brothers in the back seat taught him how to hum loudly.
Big Doug: 'What does that sign mean?' Learner: 'That the road is about to get dramatic?' Big Doug: 'Close. Read the handbook again, bud.'
Big Doug's twenty-year count: a thousand learners, four thousand roundabouts and exactly one learner who picked the right exit on the first lap. He still talks about her.
A learner asked Big Doug how he stays so calm. He said 'deep breaths and twenty years of practice.' Then he quietly put his hoof back on the handle.
Big Doug's passenger-seat posture has three settings: relaxed, alert and 'antlers pressed flat against the roof.'
Big Doug says every learner goes through three moods: 'this is easy,' 'this is impossible' and, finally, 'wait, I'm actually doing it.' Beauty.
Big Doug doesn't own a phone, but twenty years in the passenger seat gave him one superpower: he can hear a group chat buzzing inside a backpack.
Big Doug's most dreaded sign: 'No Services Next Exit.' Not because it's scary. Because the learner always looks at a quarter tank and says 'we're fine.'
My study timer says 25 minutes. My brain says 'what if we reorganized the desk first?' The desk has never looked better.
My study plan has three steps: open the handbook, read one page, reward myself with a snack. I'm very, very good at step three.
Practice quizzes are scrimmages. Nobody is keeping score except you, and you are way too hard on yourself.
Studying a little every day sounds boring. So does brushing your teeth. Both work.
Every practice quiz has one question that looks easy and is not. It's the black ice of the test: totally fine until it isn't.
The night before the test I said 'one last look at the handbook.' Two hours later I was reading the copyright page.
Studying in small chunks is like eating a whole bag of chips one at a time. Somehow it all gets done.
Parents: 'How's studying going?' Me: 'Good.' The practice quiz: 'Six out of ten.' Technically, we're both being honest.
Back-to-school shopping: new binder, new pens, new plan to stay organized. See you in October, binder.
My study spot has a desk, a lamp and a good chair. My actual study spot is the end of the couch with one sock on.
The library is the only place where a dropped pencil sounds like a firework.
Studying with a friend works best when one of you asks the questions and the other one isn't holding a phone. Switch every ten questions.
A practice test is the warm-up lap. Find the bumps now, while nobody's counting.
My mom texts like she's writing a letter: 'Dear Son. Supper is ready. Love, Mom.' We are in the same house.
Grandma texts with one finger and full sentences, and somehow she still replies faster than my whole group chat.
The charging cable at home works fine. The charging cable in the car works only at one very specific angle while nobody breathes.
Minus 40 at the bus stop: your eyelashes freeze, your phone gives up and your soul switches to power-saving mode.
A 'Pavement Ends' sign is the road saying 'the rest is between you and your suspension.'
The 'Road Narrows' sign is the road sucking in its stomach for a photo.
An 'Uneven Pavement' sign in Alberta is basically a welcome sign.
'Bridge Ices Before Road' is the most Canadian sign ever. Even the bridge needs a toque.
A 'Detour' sign is the road saying 'trust me, I know a guy.'
The 'Two-Way Traffic' sign is the road reminding you it's a group project.
The 'Narrow Bridge' sign is a bridge politely asking everybody to tuck their elbows in.
The checkerboard sign at the end of a road is the road's version of 'game over, please turn around.'
Reverse parking is regular parking with trust issues.
Every parking lot has one concrete pillar placed exactly where your mirror wants to be.
Parkade ramps are the closest thing to a corkscrew rollercoaster, and the ticket machine at the bottom is the final boss.
Angle parking looks easy until you realize the angle is a matter of opinion.
Nothing humbles you faster than parking perfectly between the lines and then reading the sign that says 'Staff Only.'
Parallel parking is a puzzle where every piece is a car and one of the pieces is shaking slightly.
My dad's calm voice is scarier than his loud voice. 'Okay. Let's just. Pull in. Right here. Nice and easy.'
Mom: 'You're doing great.' Also Mom: quietly turning off the radio so she can concentrate on my driving.
Dad's favourite question during a lesson: 'What are you looking at?' The answer, every single time: 'The road, Dad.'
Mom's driving lessons are mostly breathing exercises. Hers, not mine.
My parents argue about who's the better driving teacher. I vote for whoever brings snacks.
Dad: 'Mirror, signal, shoulder check.' Me: 'I know.' Dad: 'Say it anyway.' Me: 'Mirror, signal, shoulder check.' Dad: 'Beautiful.' It's a whole ritual now.
The parent in the passenger seat is the only person who can say 'you're fine' in a voice that clearly means 'we'll discuss this later.'
My mom practises her calm face in the visor mirror before every lesson. Very convincing. Right up until the first intersection.
My stepdad's whole teaching method is pointing. Mirror: point. Sign: point. Gopher: very enthusiastic point.
Grandpa: 'Back in my day we didn't have backup cameras.' Me: 'What did you use?' Grandpa: 'Your grandma. She'd lean out the window and yell.'
Little brother: 'Are you a good driver yet?' Me: 'I'm a learning driver.' Little brother: 'So no.' Me: 'So learning.'
Block heater cords lying in the snow all winter look like orange spaghetti that nobody is ever going to cook.
Every Alberta winter has one morning when the car door freezes shut and you seriously consider climbing in through the trunk.
Ice fog is the sky deciding to be a cloud, but low, and right in your driveway.
Sun dogs in winter: the sun brings two backup suns because one clearly isn't getting the job done at minus 35.
Spring in Edmonton is the snowbanks slowly giving back everything people lost in November. Mittens. Toques. One whole hockey stick.
A magpie sat on our side mirror for ten minutes this morning. I'm pretty sure it was supervising.
Magpies strut around parking lots with the confidence of a bird that has never once been told no.
Road salt season: every car in Alberta turns the same crusty grey. You can only tell them apart by the bumper stickers.
Hail in July sounds like the whole sky is making popcorn on your car roof.
Gophers vanish all winter. Then on the first warm day there are four hundred of them, standing up, acting like they never left.
Alberta construction detours change so often the orange signs should come with a version number.
Road trip to Drumheller: hours of flat prairie, then the ground just drops away like the map forgot a page.
Road trip I spy in Saskatchewan: 'I spy something flat.' Everyone guesses right. Every time.
A road trip cooler is a magic box. You pack sandwiches, and three hours later it's mostly melted ice and one floating pickle.
Packing the car for a road trip is a game of Tetris where the last piece is always a pillow that doesn't fit anywhere.
The back seat on a road trip has its own time zone. It's always 'how much longer?' o'clock.
Highway 2 between Edmonton and Calgary: flat, flat, Gasoline Alley, flat, and the same red barn you swear you've already passed.
Why was the stop sign so good at keeping secrets? It never let anything slide.
What's a parking lot's favourite kind of music? Anything with a lot of rests.
Why do snowplows have so many friends? They clear the way for everybody.
What did the windshield say to the ice scraper? 'You really know how to break the ice.'
Why was the roundabout so good at debates? It always came back around to its point.
Why don't Alberta potholes ever get lonely? There's always another one just up the road.
Why did the snowbank break up with the plow? It was tired of being pushed around.
Why did the block heater get invited to every party? It always plugs in and warms the place up.
Phone storage full again. It's four thousand screenshots of things I promised to look at later.
Learner: 'Big Doug, have you ever seen a perfect drive?' Big Doug: 'Twice. One was yours, just now. Don't let it go to your head.'
After twenty years riding shotgun, Big Doug can spot a nervous parent by their coffee. White knuckles, full cup, not one sip the whole drive.
Big Doug's rule for any learner's first drive: nobody mentions parallel parking. Not today. Today is about finding the wipers on purpose.
